overview: Iguanodon bernissartensis was the second dinosaur formally described — named by Gideon Mantell in 1825 from teeth found in Sussex — and one of the three genera that Richard Owen used to define Dinosauria in 1842. In 1878 coal miners in Bernissart, Belgium discovered 38 nearly complete skeletons, providing the first opportunity for scientists to study a dinosaur in full and transforming palaeontology.

For over a century Iguanodon was reconstructed walking upright like a kangaroo, with the famous thumb spike placed on the nose as a horn. Modern analysis shows it walked on four legs with the body held horizontally, and the thumb spike was a true defensive weapon — or possibly a tool for foraging. At 10 metres and 4 tonnes it was one of the largest Early Cretaceous herbivores.

articles.title: The Bernissart discovery
articles.body: Coal miners at the Sainte-Barbe pit in Bernissart hit a pocket of clay rich in dinosaur skeletons at a depth of 322 metres in 1878. Paleontologist Louis Dollo supervised the excavation and reconstruction of the animals over the following decades. The resulting mounted skeletons — 30 of which are now displayed at the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences in Brussels — gave scientists their first view of a complete ornithopod, though Dollo's erect bipedal reconstruction stood for decades before being corrected.

articles.title: The thumb spike
articles.body: Mantell initially placed the thumb spike on Iguanodon's nose as a rhinoceros-like horn — this was immortalised in the Crystal Palace statues of 1853 which still stand in London. The correct position on the thumb was established only when articulated Bernissart skeletons showed the spike attached to the first digit. Its function — defensive weapon, foraging tool for breaking open fruit, or intraspecific combat — is still debated.

articles.title: Locomotion
articles.body: The wrist bones of Iguanodon form a fused, weight-bearing structure suited to quadrupedal locomotion. Modern analysis confirms it walked primarily on all fours with the body held horizontally, rearing bipedally only to reach higher vegetation. Its dental battery — cheek teeth capable of grinding — represents an advance over the simpler teeth of Camptosaurus, foreshadowing the efficient grinding dentition of hadrosaurs.

record.mya: late Barremian-early Aptian, roughly 126-122 million years ago for I. bernissartensis
record.description: Iguanodon bernissartensis was a large herbivorous iguanodontian best known from the Bernissart mine in Belgium, where numerous associated skeletons and skulls were recovered. Modern revision restricts Iguanodon more narrowly than older books that placed many Early Cretaceous species from Europe and elsewhere in the genus.
facts: The thumb spike was on the hand, not the nose as in the earliest reconstruction.
Forelimb and hand anatomy support habitual quadrupedal walking with facultative bipedality.
The Bernissart assemblage contains multiple individuals but does not by itself prove a permanent herd.

presentation.heroLead: A large, thumb-spiked plant-eater known from dozens of associated skeletons recovered from a Belgian coal mine, making it one of the best-documented ornithopods.

animalParagraphs: Iguanodon bernissartensis was a bulky ornithopod with a long, deep skull ending in a toothless beak, batteries of leaf-shaped cheek teeth and a heavy tail stiffened by ossified tendons. Its most famous feature is a conical thumb spike, once mistakenly placed on the nose, whose function remains debated.

The forelimbs are long and stout, with a wrist bound by fused bones and three central fingers that bore hoof-like claws. This anatomy supports habitual walking on all fours, while the powerful hindlimbs indicate that the animal could also rear or move bipedally when needed.

Because more than thirty individuals were recovered from the Sainte-Barbe Clays at Bernissart, palaeontologists can study variation between animals of the same species. The length and mass figures quoted for Iguanodon are still estimates: they are scaled from mounted skeletons rather than measured from living animals.
animalHighlights: A conical thumb spike on each hand is the signature feature; its use in defence, feeding or display is interpretation rather than observation.
Cheek teeth with ridged crowns and a mobile upper jaw allowed the animal to grind plant material, an unusually sophisticated chewing system for a reptile.
Robust forelimbs and hoof-like middle fingers show that Iguanodon habitually walked on four legs, with bipedal movement available.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.level: Directly evidenced by teeth and jaws
lifeCards.reason: Dense batteries of worn cheek teeth and a horny beak are preserved on many skulls. Which plants were eaten is not recorded by gut contents.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Hand and wrist anatomy support weight-bearing on the forelimbs; how often the animal walked on two legs is inferred, not observed.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Numerous near-complete individuals constrain proportions well, but mass estimates of roughly three to four tonnes depend on the modelling method used.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Proportions are among the best known for any dinosaur. Skin texture, colour and any soft-tissue crests are not preserved for this species.

locality.name: Bernissart colliery
locality.note: Sainte-Barbe Clays Formation, encountered in 1878 at a depth of more than 300 metres in the Sainte-Barbe pit. The map plots the village of Bernissart rather than the mine shaft.

presentation.classificationSummary: Iguanodon is a styracosternan iguanodontian, part of the lineage leading towards hadrosaurs. Modern revisions restrict the genus to I. bernissartensis and a few close relatives; many species once called Iguanodon are now placed in other genera such as Mantellisaurus.

questions.title: What was the thumb spike for?
questions.copy: Defence, breaking into plant food and intraspecific combat have all been proposed. None is directly testable from the fossils.

questions.title: Did Iguanodon live in herds?
questions.copy: The Bernissart animals were buried together, but the deposit may have accumulated over time. It does not by itself prove permanent group living.

questions.title: Which species belong in the genus?
questions.copy: Only I. bernissartensis is uncontroversial. Some historical European specimens and I. galvensis from Spain remain difficult to assign with confidence.

review.ageReviewNote: I. bernissartensis is late Barremian-early Aptian; older broad genus ranges largely reflect reassigned species.

Modern revision restricts Iguanodon more narrowly than older books that placed many Early Cretaceous species from Europe and elsewhere in the genus.

specimens.institution: Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences, Brussels
specimens.note: Near-complete articulated skeleton from Bernissart, designated neotype of I. bernissartensis by ICZN Opinion 1947 (2000) in place of the fragmentary English type material of the genus.

specimens.name: Bernissart referred skeletons
specimens.institution: Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences, Brussels
specimens.note: More than thirty individuals from the Sainte-Barbe Clays; many articulated, several mounted.

panel.headline: Dozens of associated skeletons from a single Belgian coal mine.
panel.standfirst: Iguanodon bernissartensis is known from more than thirty individuals recovered at Bernissart between 1878 and 1881, many of them articulated and near complete, together with skulls, hands, feet and ossified tail tendons.

coverage.label: Excellent
coverage.basis: Every region of the skeleton, including the skull, hands, feet and tail, is represented by multiple articulated individuals from the Bernissart assemblage.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: Articulated skulls with tooth batteries, complete vertebral columns with ossified tendons, shoulder and hip girdles, and full forelimbs and hindlimbs including the spiked hands and three-toed feet, all from many individuals.
knownRemains.note: The Belgian material is extraordinarily complete, but pyrite decay has damaged some bones since excavation, and specimens from England and Spain referred to the genus are far less complete.

media.title: Bernissart Iguanodon mounted in a quadrupedal pose
media.alt: Mounted skeleton of Iguanodon bernissartensis in a four-legged pose in Brussels
media.caption: One of the Bernissart skeletons displayed at the Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences, Brussels, mounted in the modern quadrupedal posture. The historic mounts in the same hall retain the upright pose favoured by Louis Dollo.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Numerous complete skulls with beaks, dental batteries and braincases, allowing detailed study of jaw mechanics.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Complete cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal series with ribs and lattices of ossified tendons along the back and tail.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Complete shoulder and pelvic girdles; forelimbs with fused wrists, thumb spikes and hoofed fingers; hindlimbs and three-toed feet.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Articulated, associated skeletons and ossified tendons; no skin, gut contents or colour are preserved for this species.

specimenCards.title: IRSNB 1534 · neotype
specimenCards.description: A near-complete articulated skeleton from Bernissart, designated the neotype of Iguanodon bernissartensis by the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature in 2000 to anchor the genus to the Belgian material.
specimenCards.meta: Bernissart · Sainte-Barbe Clays Formation · Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences

specimenCards.title: The Bernissart skeletons
specimenCards.description: Dozens of individuals of varying size recovered from two bone-bearing levels in the mine; about two dozen are mounted or displayed in Brussels. Verdú and colleagues used this sample to document individual variation within one species.
specimenCards.meta: Excavated 1878–1881 · Royal Belgian Institute of Natural Sciences

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Complete skulls, dental batteries, articulated skeletons, thumb spikes, hoof-like fingers and ossified tendons from many individuals.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: Habitual quadrupedal walking with facultative bipedality, sophisticated grinding of plant food, and a body mass of a few tonnes scaled from the mounts.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Skin texture and colour, the purpose of the thumb spike, whether the animals lived in herds, and the assignment of some historical specimens from outside Belgium.
